clinicalPearls: DFNB loci underlie the majority of severe congenital hereditary sensorineural hearing loss, usually presenting prelingually
Inheritance is autosomal recessive, so parents are typically unaffected carriers and consanguinity increases risk
DFNB1 (GJB2/GJB6) is by far the commonest locus, but many other genes such as SLC26A4, MYO15A, and OTOF contribute
Most forms are stable, though SLC26A4-related DFNB4 (with enlarged vestibular aqueduct) fluctuates and progresses
The phenotype is usually bilateral and symmetrical without systemic features, distinguishing it from syndromic deafness
Vestibular involvement is uncommon in most loci but occurs with particular genes
Early identification enables timely amplification or cochlear implantation with generally good language outcomes
reference.pathophysiology: The DFNB group encompasses numerous loci in which biallelic loss-of-function variants disrupt proteins essential to cochlear development or function, including gap-junction proteins, hair cell stereocilia and motor proteins, and ion transporters. Because both alleles must be affected, heterozygous carriers are typically asymptomatic and disease appears in the offspring of two carriers. The resulting lesion is usually cochlear and often severe and congenital, reflecting failure of hair cell mechanotransduction, endolymph homeostasis, or synaptic transmission depending on the gene involved. The central auditory pathway is generally intact, which is why direct cochlear stimulation is effective.
additionalDifferentials: Syndromic recessive hearing loss (Usher, Pendred, Jervell and Lange-Nielsen)
Auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder including OTOF-related forms
Inner-ear malformations such as incomplete partition
Autosomal dominant (DFNA) hearing loss where inheritance is unclear
Acquired perinatal ototoxic or hypoxic injury
additionalInvestigations: Newborn screening followed by diagnostic behavioural or objective audiometry
Otoacoustic emissions and auditory brainstem response to define the lesion
Deafness gene panel or exome sequencing beginning with DFNB1 testing
Temporal bone imaging to detect malformations and plan implantation
Congenital cytomegalovirus testing to exclude an acquired cause
Assessment for syndromic features including ophthalmology, thyroid, renal, and cardiac review as indicated
redFlags: Progression or fluctuation suggesting SLC26A4-related disease with an enlarged vestibular aqueduct
Emerging visual, thyroid, renal, or cardiac features indicating a syndrome
Delayed speech and language from under-recognised loss
Cardiac syncope or prolonged QT raising concern for Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome
reference.prognosis: Most DFNB forms are stable, and with early amplification or cochlear implantation and structured habilitation children typically develop good spoken language; fluctuating SLC26A4-related disease carries a more variable course.
pitfalls: Stopping at a single GJB2 variant without excluding a GJB6 deletion or another locus
Missing an evolving syndrome by not screening for extra-auditory features
Overlooking congenital cytomegalovirus as a treatable or coexisting cause
Delaying intervention while awaiting complete genetic results
references: GeneReviews: Nonsyndromic Hearing Loss and Deafness, Genetic Overview
